summary: Reframe gravity from 'the force that makes things fall on Earth' to a universal attractive force acting between all masses everywhere — the same force pulling an apple down holds the Moon to Earth and planets to the Sun. Two strands do the KS3 heavy lifting: (1) orbits as 'falling sideways' (Newton's cannonball) — an orbiting body is continuously falling toward the central body but moving sideways fast enough to keep missing, so its path curves into a closed loop; and (2) weight vs field strength, weight = mass × g, where mass is invariant but g differs between planets. Tackle 'there is no gravity in space' head-on: astronauts float not because gravity is absent (in a low orbit like the International Space Station's it is still about 90% as strong as at the surface) but because they and their spacecraft are in continuous free fall together.
misconceptions: There is no gravity in space / astronauts float because there is no gravity (they are in free fall; gravity in orbit is nearly as strong as at the surface)
Gravity only acts downward on Earth, or only large/special objects like planets have gravity (all masses attract all masses)
Mass and weight are the same thing / your mass changes on the Moon (mass is constant; only weight, = mass × g, changes)
Orbiting objects are 'balancing' gravity with an outward force, or gravity switches off in orbit (orbit is continuous free fall; the only force is inward gravity)
Gravity requires air / there is no gravity without an atmosphere
Heavier objects fall faster (in free fall, acceleration due to gravity is the same regardless of mass)

activities.title: Newton's cannonball: tune launch speed until it orbits
steps: Set a launch speed for a cannonball fired horizontally from the top of a tall mountain and predict where it will land before firing.
Fire at a gentle speed and watch it arc out and hit the ground a short distance away.
Nudge the speed higher repeatedly, observing the ball land further each time and the curve of its fall starting to echo the curve of the planet.
Find the critical speed at which the ball falls all the way around without reaching the ground and loops back — a stable orbit.
Push faster still to stretch the circle into an ellipse, then faster again until the ball escapes entirely.
In your own words, state what the ball is actually doing when it orbits (it is only falling — it is just going sideways fast enough to keep missing the Earth).
activities.insight: An orbit is continuous free fall: in this idealised model (no air resistance), the only force is gravity pulling inward, curving otherwise-straight sideways motion into a closed loop. Too slow and the ball arcs down and hits the ground; from the circular-orbit speed up to just below escape speed it orbits (a circle at first, then longer ellipses as speed rises); at or above escape speed it leaves for good. Orbit is continuous with everyday falling, not a separate phenomenon.

activities.title: Same mass, different weight: weight = mass × g across worlds
steps: Stand a fixed mass on a scale and read its weight on Earth.
Switch the planet selector to the Moon, then Jupiter, each time reading the new weight while noting the mass number never changes.

Using weight = mass × g (with g ≈ 10 N/kg on Earth), calculate the weight of a 40 kg mass on Earth; then work out its weight on the Moon using the Moon's g ≈ 1.6 N/kg, and compare with a hypothetical world of half Earth's g.
State explicitly what changed (weight, because g changed) and what stayed the same (mass, the amount of matter).
activities.insight: Mass (amount of matter) is invariant; weight = mass × g changes because gravitational field strength g differs between planets. The same astronaut weighs less on the Moon though their mass is unchanged.

activities.title: Free fall explains floating: drop the whole station
steps: Toggle the cannon-and-station into free fall and watch the astronaut inside floating.
Note that the gravity indicator shows gravity fully on the whole time — nothing has switched off.
Explain why the astronaut floats: they and the station are falling together, so there is nothing to press them against a floor.
Predict what path the station would follow if gravity really were zero (a straight line off into space, not a circle).
activities.insight: Astronauts float because they and their spacecraft are in continuous free fall together, not because gravity is absent — in a low orbit like the ISS's, gravity is about 90% as strong as at the surface. Gravity provides the centripetal (inward) force; remove it and the station would fly off in a straight line.

activities.title: Talk it through with an astronaut in orbit (Socratic dialogue)
steps: Pose the question to an in-role astronaut character: 'Is there gravity up here? Why do you float if gravity is still pulling you?'
Offer your own explanation and have the character probe it with follow-up questions.
Revise your reasoning toward: gravity is present and strong, and floating is because everything is in free fall together.
activities.insight: The 'no gravity in space' belief is verbal and sticky; articulating and defending reasoning aloud can help surface and challenge it. The goal is to replace 'gravity is absent' with 'we are falling around the Earth'.

activities.title: Universality: the same force everywhere
steps: Examine a two-mass attraction diagram showing the force acting on BOTH bodies (apple–Earth, Earth–Moon, Sun–planet).
State the common rule: every mass attracts every other mass; the pull is stronger for bigger masses and weaker the farther apart they are.
Explain why we do not notice the pull between two everyday objects (it is real but far too weak to feel), and why planets' pull is obvious (huge mass).
Decide whether gravity could act in a vacuum with no air, and justify the answer.
activities.insight: Gravity is universal: the same attractive force operates between an apple and Earth, Earth and Moon, Sun and planets; it is stronger for larger masses and weaker at greater distances. It is not special to Earth's surface, does not require an atmosphere, and acts equally on both bodies in a pair.

activities.title: Check and consolidate: weight calculations and the orbit diagnostic
steps: Complete weight = mass × g calculations for a fixed mass on different planets (give the missing weight for Earth, Moon and Jupiter).
Answer the diagnostic: 'Astronauts on the Space Station float as if weightless. Does that mean there is no gravity up there? Explain what is really keeping the station in orbit.'

Give the two-part answer: there IS gravity (roughly 90% of surface strength at the Station), and floating is because the station and astronauts are in continuous free fall, with gravity supplying the inward (centripetal) force that curves their motion into an orbit.
Answer the probe: 'If gravity in orbit were really zero, what path would the Station follow — a circle or a straight line?' and justify (a straight line, because no force means no curving).
activities.insight: Consolidation: apply weight = mass × g numerically and articulate orbit as continuous free fall with gravity providing the centripetal force. Both 'no gravity' and 'gravity provides the orbit' predict floating, so the reasoning must be stated to distinguish them.

checkQuestion: Astronauts on the Space Station float around as if weightless. Does that mean there is no gravity up there? … Explain what is really keeping the station in orbit.
checkAnswer: There IS gravity in orbit — at the Station's height it's roughly 90% as strong as at the surface. The astronauts float because they and the station are in continuous FREE FALL: gravity keeps pulling them toward Earth, curving their straight-line motion into an orbit — they are 'falling around' the Earth. Gravity provides the centripetal force; with no gravity they would fly off in a straight line, not orbit.
